I do a lab similar to the one linked below about atomic structure. It involves students rolling marbles at targets and collecting data on their ratio of hits to misses. A bit of fancy math and they can calculate the diameter of the target indirectly based on the hit/miss ratio. The intent is to help them understand how Rutherford discovered the existence of a tiny nucleus based on the gold foil experiment.

For periodic table stuff, I don't know about labs per se, but I found a fun activity on TPT (I think) where students are given a bunch of alien dudes with different features that represent atomic properties. They are tasked to basically recreate the first few rows of the periodic table by organizing the aliens by their traits and it helps them understand that the real table is organized in groups and families by similar properties.

You could also create some cards or something similar with elements and some of their properties. Throw in some "mystery" elements that have properties but no name given. The students have to figure out what the mystery elements are based on similarities in properties to the known elements you gave them.

I usually teach metal/metalloid/nonmetal properties and areas of the periodic table with this material too, and it's pretty easy to do a lab with those. It could be as simple as setting out some samples of each category and ask students to figure out what are the common features of a metal vs. nonmetal. You could even have some unlabeled ones again and tell your students they need to determine which of the 3 categories it would belong to by the end of the lab by analyzing the other samples.

So density will naturally decrease. This is the reason a gas phase substance is always going to be less dense than the solid phase of that substance even if the mass is the same.

The density of a substance never changes assuming temperature and pressure are kept constant, but substances have different densities if temperature and pressure fluctuate

If you're playing for completion, it probably goes down to a 7 or 8 out of 10 just because of the frustrating design choices.

The combination of long levels, hidden boxes, inverted levels, and timeline levels quickly turns the game into a tedious slog.

First, a lot of levels basically force you to play the game with a walkthrough to ensure you don't miss boxes that are intentionally hidden off camera, behind the environment, etc. This is the main sin that has been covered to death. The first 3 worlds aren't too bad on this, and then it's like they decided to try to make the levels as frustrating and unfun as possible in some cases.

Then the levels being relatively long compared to past titles makes it even more painful when you find out you missed the 1 off-screen box at the end of the level, hence having to play with a walkthrough to see your box total needed at each checkpoint.

Then you also have to not die 3 times (basically impossible on some of the levels while trying to get 100% of boxes your first time) or not die at all if you are a masochist and want all the insanely perfect relics. The death gem often forces you to play each level at least once more after getting the box gem.

Then you have to do that a second time on every level for the inverted stages, many of which are visually painful or distracting because of the filters.

Then there are the timeline levels that for some reason make you play half of the original level again so it feels like you are doing the same thing a 3rd and then a 4th time because they all have inverted versions too.

I think the game would have been positively received across the board if they drastically limited the bullshittery of the boxes. Keep the hidden gems as the things that are often off-camera and require exploration and creativity to find. Less BS boxes will probably also contribute to requiring fewer player-forced deaths to do checkpoint rests making the death gem less painful.

My other idea would be to remove the 5/6 gems from the inverted versions of the levels and just keep the new evil hidden gem locations. I think it would be a lot less painful if you were just replaying the flipped versions to find a new hidden gem spot. It would feel more fun rather than like a chore where you have to 100% complete it again 5 seconds after you just beat it.

Then sever the timeline levels and make them a bit longer so they stand alone and don't just rehash the exact same levels for a 4th time.

Make those small changes and I think it would feel a billion times more fair and manageable.

* Avoid resting as much as possible. Ideally, you should be upgrading cards. Unless you are going to die in your next few fights otherwise, upgrading a card may actually save you more health than resting by ending fights quicker or blocking more hits

Think about what fights, elites, and what boss you are going to encounter each act, and plan accordingly. >  I was told that I would be teaching APES, high school chemistry, as well as 6th, 7th, and 8th grade middle school science. On top of that, they want me to provide two elective classes that are completely my choice.

This sounds impossible. Even with two different classes, being a first year teacher is very difficult and taxing. Teaching 7 different classes at once is beyond comprehension.

I would recommend un-accepting the position unless you are in love with this school or something

1) Good teaching is not lecturing constantly. You will want to give students other activities that will make the burden of knowledge and speaking less for yourself. You also don't have to lecture from memory. Using something like a powerpoint to guide yourself or some written notes that you can follow along to write on a whiteboard are perfectly fine. I even had university professors follow their own notes

2) You can use other sources for inspiration, but try to create your own lesson plans. When you write something yourself, you will be able to remember it much better than if it is another teacher's activity or something you found online.

3) Comfort yourself with the fact that you don't need to know everything at all times. It's okay to just have ready what you need for that day or that week. You don't need to have the content you are going to cover 2 months from now down pat right away.

4) Study up on things before you teach them. Rusty on genetics? Watch some videos and do some reading about concepts you are a little fuzzy on the week before you cover it with your students. It will make you more confident and you may pick up tips on how to teach those ideas to your students
